en: Unbeliever and Muslim
Gave their blessings together.
My little soul conceived through blessings,
Gray-maned khan gone to the other world,
Look upon the orphan!
Host of saints and holy elders,
Give the orphan your protection!
My strength has failed from being beaten.
O God, I stand here bereft.
Hailstones have fallen upon my head;
O God, I stand here wasted away.
Scarcely any blood remains in my body;
No strength remains when I try to walk.
There is no forest to flee into;
No Nogai to give us support,
I have no ridge to put my trust in;
I have no sheltered place.
Finding no cliff that a goose cannot circle,
Finding no inaccessible dark mountain,
I stand here in grief!”
Thus your sister-in-law wept,
Her heart terribly distraught,
Tears pouring from her eyes,
Her limbs giving way as she sobbed.
Turning, weeping and crying aloud,
To Uch-Koshoy's Chatkal
Your sister-in-law came running.
Karymbay's brown calf, nursed by a cow that had not calved again,
A calf fostered by two mothers,
Had been driven away by gadflies
And left at the deserted camp.
“Look at my tears, God;
Give me the brown calf, God!”
May that calf tumble down!
When it saw Kanykey,
It fled downhill, slipping and sliding.
When it saw Kanykey,
May that calf tumble down!
It fled uphill in a frenzy.
Then your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
Her wide world grown narrow,
Longing for the brown calf,
Could not catch it in pursuit.
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Tears fell drop after drop.
From her dear currant-like eyes,
Tears ran a whip's length.
Kanykey pondered a plan:
“If I could catch and slaughter the calf,
If I could feed my orphan just once!”
May that calf tumble down!
It scampered about the mountain.
Your tormented sister-in-law Kanykey
Pursued it, crying aloud.
Karymbay's calf
Scampered along the ridge.
Struggling to chase the calf,
Hard pressed and unable to catch it,
Your sister-in-law went on sobbing and weeping.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey,
Around the lower slopes of Uch-Koshoy,
Chased it three times;
Around the sweep of Beles-Tash,
Chased it five times.
Your heroic sister-in-law Kanykey
Stood gathering courage.
“The fate God has imposed
Is like this; let me face it.
Rather than groan and starve in the plain,
Rather than endure this humiliation,
Let me die chasing the calf.
O God, if I could chase it down and slaughter it,
My mother who has grown old,
At least, oh world,
I could give her some relief.”
Around Uyurulmo's Chatkal
She chased it three times.
Karymbay's brown calf
Scampered away in flight.
Your dear mother Kanykey
Pursued without tiring, crying aloud.
Along Uch-Koshoy,
At Batkaktuu's spring-fed stream,
The calf tried to cross and became stuck.
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykey
Fell upon it, pinning it down.
Your dear mother Kanykey
Caught it and led it away.
To where Chyyyrdy and Semetey
Were lying, she took the shortest path.
She took the calf along,
Leading it toward her orphan.
As she was about to reach the orphan,
On a red chestnut horse,
Its long-haired tail tied in a tight knot,
A banner floating in his hand,
A battle-axe flashing in his hand,
A blue spear swaying in his hand,
White foam mixed with blood
Squishing at his stirrups,
His iron fittings shaking,
His gun for entering battle
Bobbing at his other side,
He towered in fury,
His nose bulging like a wineskin,
Their figures unfolded,
Looking like the Ala-Too mountains.
Among the Argyns and Kyrgyz,
He was a man of sound intelligence,
Yet without a trace of humanity,
There was one called Karymbay.
“When Jet-Kayt was humiliated,
When Manas married your sister-in-law,
They held a feast for sixty days.
The peoples of the world gathered;
Yesterday, crunching sugar white as snow,
Sipping black tea,
While they were drinking their fill,
Well-fattened lambs and sweet-tasting heads,
They set them boiling vigorously,
Yearling colts nursed by mares that had not foaled again
Were slaughtered for their midday meal.
They measured out forty foot-lengths;
Forty mares for each place
Were staked as prizes.
Aykhojo in his motley coat
Was chosen to serve as mullah.
Play a fun game,
They played chess, raising a commotion.
Sixty khojas and forty eshens
Were chosen as judges.
When all the khojas were gathered,
When the marriage rite joined me to my prince,
The gold, with a horse at the head of the gifts,
You received as an impartial witness.
You were my ceremonial father;
Karymbay, I was your ceremonial daughter.
You who ate flour of white wheat,
Whom I held closer than my father,
You were my ceremonial father.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
Give me your calf without begrudging it;
Give me your calf to slaughter.
In her bereft old age,
Let me feed my mother once.”
“Ceremonial father Karymbay,
When I try to walk, my strength fails;
Black blood flows from my calves.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
I have been wandering from the beginning;
I was parted from my Bloodstained One
At thirty-two years of age.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
I have wasted away; restore my flesh.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
Fill my hungry belly.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
If your heart inclines, give me water.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
If your heart does not incline,
Pour poison in a leather flask and give me that.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
My flame has gone out; kindle it.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
I am dying; bring me back to life.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
Join together what has broken in me.
I have scattered; gather me up.
I am thirsty; give me tea.
Let me hide my head;
Give me a place to shelter.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
A shot has wounded my ankle;
I stand unable to turn.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
A shot has pierced across my ribs;
I stand unable to turn around.
The ground I tread has become a cliff;
My own kin have become enemies.
All the slaves have run mad;
They raided my moving camp at Keng-Kol.
The boy who could speak for me is young;
I cannot take my vengeance on the dogs.
In the infidel's iron-rope
I am caught in his net, Karymbay.
Knowing not a hair of deceit,
My low-born kinsman's
Hands hold me captive, Karymbay.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
Give me six fat horses;
Give me six skins of milk.
Weeping aloud in the plain,
What wish shall I fulfill?
When a woman's husband dies,
Her own kin become close to her.
Let me wander off to Karakan.
My orphan left by the Magnanimous One,
If he grows into a vigorous man,
If he becomes the equal of other men's sons,
If he becomes a lion like his father,
If he grows to maturity as an orphan,
If he joins the ranks of the people,
If God lets us see Talas again,
If he becomes a khan with his own court,
If he becomes a settled, steadfast son,
I shall send word to my people.
If I come back to the Kyrgyz,
Or at least to the Argyns,
I shall raise him up as khan.
Ceremonial father Karymbay,
Clothe me entirely in silk;
Mount me on an excellent pacer.
What shall I do staying here?
Let me wander off to Temir Khan!
Find me your coat of dressed hide and give it;
Choose a horse from your swiftest and give it!”
With hands clasped, imploring,
She stood weeping and crying aloud.
Your mother Kanykey
Threw herself upon Karymbay's mercy,
Pleading with all her strength.
Ceremonial father Karymbay
Did not heed her pleas,
Nor would he agree to her staying;
He did not give the brown calf.
The sacred writing tied in his belt struck him;
The oath sworn by God struck Karymbay.
Pure in the Prophet-sultan's faith,
The sovereign God struck him.
Raging without restraint,
A demon possessed the slave Karymbay.
Tossing his mustache,
Karymbay surged forward.
He blustered, working himself up,
Speaking at Kanykey,
His face drained of blood as he roared.
What could your sister-in-law Kanykey do?
She stood trembling in fear.
“You fierce woman, when you were a girl,
You stirred the ages and disrupted the people.
You fierce woman, when you were a wife,
You overturned customs and disrupted the people.
Yesterday, when you reached fourteen,
You put a sheath upon your sword.
When you reached fourteen years of age,
You struck Manas and wounded him,
And stirred up a quarrel among all the people.
I will not agree to what you say.
Let the calf go, woman;
I will not give you my calf.
A widow still running wild,
Who will not give up her mischief,
With Manas's white-headed horses in the foothills,
You were not satisfied with his many livestock.
Manas had a treasury of gold coins;
At all times this woman
